title: Unpredictable interaction with CloseWatcher anti-trapping & hover popovers
body:
### What is the issue with the HTML Standard?

# Demonstration

Example of what I'm talking about (source code): https://gitlab.com/sampointon/closewatcher-anti-trap-hover

Steps to reproduce:
0. Clone the repo, run a local server serving the reproducer (e.g., `python -m http.server` in the repo directory) and navigate to `main.html`.
1. Click on the button to open a popover.
2. Hover over the button inside the popover.
3. Press Escape.
4. Observe that the hover-triggered popover is closed.
5. Hover over the button again.
6. Press Escape.
7. Observe that _both_ popovers close this time.

(You may need to repeat steps 4-6 if you interact with the page, e.g. by clicking elsewhere. Eventually step 7 will happen as the page runs out of user interaction credit.)

Since this relies on CloseWatcher, it'll only work out of the box on Chromium, but AFAICT Chromium is behaving as specced.

# The problem

What gets closed is unpredictable to the user: the same action (pressing Escape) in one instance only closes the hover popover, and in the next instance it closes both popovers.

# Analysis

For anti-trapping behaviour, the browser keeps count of how many times a user has 'heavily' interacted with the page (e.g., clicked, rather than just moused around) and, if a user performs a close-requesting action (pressing Escape, the Android swipe-to-dismiss motion) too many times relative to that count, _every_ close watcher (including implicit close watchers created by auto popovers) gets a close signal rather than just the topmost. This is necessary because some close-requesting actions will also do things like navigate away from the page if there's no close watcher on the page to intercept and consume the close request (e.g., Android's swipe to dismiss will move back in history), and it'd be bad if a page could swallow them with no recourse, and so the anti-trapping behaviour is very justified.

For things that are opened with a heavy-enough-to-count-as-a-user-interaction interaction like `<button popovertarget>`, this is fine and great. The problem is with things that use lighter interactions - like hover. As demonstrated, using close watchers for these leads to unpredictable behaviour (which is bad!), but not using close watchers means missing out on platform integration (e.g., there's no other way of listening for Android's swipe to dismiss). For the time being, AIUI, it's probably fine to just listen for Escape keypresses, which are the only other common type of close request, but that's hardly future proof and it's kind of ugly that, even with a purpose-built API for listening for close requests, it's not usable for this. (Not listening at all to close requests of some flavour is not an option due to [WCAG 1.4.13](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#content-on-hover-or-focus).)

As the demo above shows, this is already a problem you can run in to (I certainly did!), but with #10309 in mind it'd be nice to have a solution so that doing the obvious thing will Just Work (especially since interest invokers are hopefully going to be 100% declarative in many common cases).

# Suggestion

A new variant of a close watcher specifically for closing things opened with light interactions, which does _not_ consume the close request, but which rather fires its close event and then passes the close request down to the next layer. These non-consuming close watchers will not need to count for anti-trapping behaviour.

(I also think they'd be useful in a couple of other places, also related to #10309 and hover, including race conditions where there's a stack of auto popovers and a hover popover, the user has hovered away and then pressed Escape, and the hovered-away timer is racing against that keypress: it'd be nice to guarantee that the resulting state is the same no matter which wins the race, and this suggestion guarantees that the topmost auto popover always gets closed. But that's a different issue and a separate motivator.)
